name: Off-Chain Governance
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Rough Consensus and Running Code
lesson.summary: Off-chain governance keeps proposal debate and decision-making in human venues like mailing lists, forums, and developer calls, and relies on node operators voluntarily choosing to run the resulting software rather than automatic on-chain execution.
lesson.body:
Off-chain governance is the older and, among the largest blockchains, still more common approach: instead of encoding voting into the protocol itself, decisions get made in human venues, mailing lists, GitHub discussions, developer calls, community forums, and conferences, and the outcome only becomes real when node operators individually choose to download and run software that implements it. Bitcoin and Ethereum both govern this way. There is no on-chain vote that activates a Bitcoin protocol change; there is a written proposal, argument about its merits, rough consensus among the people who show up to debate it, and then a race to see whether enough of the network actually adopts the resulting software.

The formal artifact of this process is the improvement proposal: a Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, or BIP, and Ethereum's equivalent, the EIP. Both are structured documents describing a proposed change, its motivation, and its technical specification, submitted to a public repository where anyone can comment. Ethereum additionally runs regular All Core Devs calls where client teams and researchers discuss which EIPs are ready for the next scheduled network upgrade. Nothing in this process is a binding vote; a proposal advances because enough of the people who matter for its adoption, client developers, validators, exchanges, and node operators, are persuaded it is worth shipping, and it dies quietly if that persuasion never arrives.

Because adoption is the real vote in an off-chain governance system, node operators retain a form of veto that on-chain governance designs away. The clearest demonstration is BIP 148, the user-activated soft fork that helped force Segregated Witness onto Bitcoin in 2017. After a long stalemate in which a significant share of mining power had not signaled support for SegWit, a coalition of businesses, developers, and users committed to running BIP 148 nodes that would reject blocks from miners who had not adopted SegWit by a set date. Facing the prospect of their blocks being orphaned by a large chunk of the economic network, miners signaled support and SegWit activated, driven not by a formal vote but by node operators and businesses threatening to reject noncompliant blocks.

When off-chain deliberation fails to produce agreement, the result is usually not gridlock but a fork, since anyone is free to copy the code and ship a competing version. The block size dispute discussed earlier in this chapter is the canonical example: after years of off-chain argument failed, part of the community forked away to create Bitcoin Cash with a larger block size, and each chain continued under the rules its own supporters chose to run. Off-chain governance does not prevent this outcome; it means the split happens through independent adoption decisions rather than a losing on-chain vote.

Compared to on-chain governance, off-chain governance is slower and less legible from the outside; there is no single ledger entry that says a proposal passed, only a gradual, sometimes ambiguous accumulation of adopted software across the network. What it buys in exchange is resistance to the plutocracy and flash-attack risks of token-weighted voting, since influence in an off-chain process depends on ongoing technical credibility and the willingness of independent node operators to actually run your code, not on how many tokens you can borrow for one vote. Most blockchains in practice, including ones with on-chain treasury votes, still fall back on off-chain deliberation for the most consequential, consensus-level changes.
